problems.description: conftest.py mutates sys.path via sys.path.insert(0, ...) and reassigns app_module.DATABASE at import time; works for a small app but couples test bootstrap to module globals. A conftest that sets DATABASE before app import or uses a session-scoped env override would be cleaner.

Mechanical convention score of 0.65 reflects 27 violations in app.py, celery_app.py, celery_config.py, __init__.py — files this commit did NOT touch (celery_app.py, celery_config.py, __init__.py are absent from the diff). The 14 new functions added (tests/conftest.py, tests/test_app.py) use snake_case and comply; the +1 cognitive complexity is in the added tests, not production logic.

strengths: Fixes a real logic bug: new tasks were created with status 'done'; corrected to 'pending', the natural initial state for a task manager API
Comprehensive test coverage — 14 tests spanning success, validation errors (missing/blank/no body), 404 paths, ordering, and update semantics
Per-test DB isolation via tempfile-backed fixture prevents cross-test contamination
Persistence test (test_create_then_persisted_in_db) verifies writes actually reach the DB, not just in-memory response state
Test-only change to production code (one-line status fix), keeping the risk surface minimal
commit_reviews.summary: A focused, low-risk commit that fixes the incorrect default task status and adds thorough, well-isolated pytest coverage; the flagged convention violations are pre-existing in files this commit did not modify, so the commit itself adheres to the codebase's conventions.

problems.description: 27 convention violations with a measured convention score of 0.65 (below the adherence bar): naming violations span the new/modified celery_app.py, celery_config.py, __init__.py (snake_case/PascalCase/UPPER_CASE) and app.py.
Mixed scope in a single feature commit: +404/-53 lines across 2 new files bundles JWT auth with a Celery addition, making review and rollback harder than a focused auth change.
JWT_SECRET_KEY falls back to a hardcoded 'dev-secret-key-change-in-production' value; if env var is unset in deployment, HS256 tokens are forgeable. Should fail closed when not configured.
Inconsistent datetime handling: deprecated datetime.utcnow() in create_task alongside datetime.now(timezone.utc) for JWT exp — should be unified on timezone-aware UTC.
Schema migration (ALTER TABLE tasks ADD owner_id) runs inside init_db guarded by PRAGMA introspection; works but couples migration logic to startup and only handles the additive column case.

strengths: Owner-scoped queries enforced on every task read/write path (WHERE owner_id = ?), preventing cross-user access via IDOR
Migration guarded by PRAGMA table_info introspection preserves existing databases without touching rows
Passwords hashed with werkzeug generate_password_hash, never stored in plaintext
JWT handling includes explicit expiry and distinct expired/invalid token errors returning 401
Auth is implemented as plain functions plus a require_auth decorator using Flask's g, matching the existing single-file function-based architecture
commit_reviews.summary: A net-positive Session 2 feature that adds JWT auth and owner scoping cleanly on top of the existing single-file Flask patterns, but is dragged down by 27 convention violations (score 0.65), a mixed auth+Celery scope, and a hardcoded dev secret fallback.

problems.description: Notification-trigger logic (status-transition guard + owner lookup + .delay call) is embedded inline in edit_task, adding +4 cognitive complexity per SonarQube; extracting it into a small helper (e.g. notify_on_completion(task, previous)) would keep the route thin and match the 'get_task/update_task' helper style used elsewhere.
Email address is synthesized as f"{username}@example.com" inside the route, coupling the handler to a fake address format; acceptable for a mock task but a named helper would localize the assumption.

Mechanical convention score of 0.65 is inflated by checker false positives: lowercase module-level names (broker_url, celery_app) and 'Classes should use PascalCase' on celery_app.py/celery_config.py are the idiomatic Celery config_from_object pattern, not violations.

strengths: Transition guard (previous is not None and previous['status'] != 'completed') makes the notification idempotent, preventing duplicate triggers on already-completed tasks.
Strong test coverage: 7 tests cover happy path, in_progress, title-only, already-completed, missing task, owner email correctness, and direct task execution.
Clean separation of concerns: celery_config.py (config), celery_app.py (app instance), tasks.py (task defs), with broker/backend URLs overridable via env vars.
Uses existing helpers (get_task, get_user_by_id, update_task) and follows the app's established route + pytest fixture patterns.
commit_reviews.summary: A well-tested, idempotent Celery integration that fits the existing task API cleanly; the only real nit is inline trigger logic in the route, and the 0.65 convention score largely reflects Celery-idiomatic lowercase config misflagged by the checker.

problems.description: Backward-compatibility shim kept only for get_user_by_username while the sibling module functions (get_user_by_id, get_tasks, get_task, fetch_task, update_task, create_task) were removed outright and their callers rewritten — an inconsistent compatibility strategy that leaves one vestigial wrapper in app.py.

Convention score of 0.65 reflects repo-wide violations (celery_app.py, celery_config.py, __init__.py snake_case/PascalCase/UPPER_CASE) that are pre-existing and untouched by this diff; the new repositories/ code itself follows naming conventions, so the low score is largely not attributable to this commit.

strengths: Clean repository layer: SQLite CRUD consolidated into BaseRepository with TaskRepository/UserRepository, removing ~90 lines of inline SQL from app.py
Passing the get_db callable (not a live connection) into repositories preserves the test suite's per-test DATABASE repointing with no stale connection/path caching
SonarQube shows zero new bugs/smells and cognitive complexity -2, confirming the refactor reduces rather than adds complexity
Parameterized queries and context-managed connections carried through consistently into the new layer
Well-documented design rationale in docstrings (db_provider swap, backward-compat shim)
Routes updated uniformly to the repository API in the same commit, so no dangling callers
commit_reviews.summary: A well-executed persistence-layer refactor that reduces complexity and improves testability with zero new defects, though the convention measurement (0.65) is dominated by pre-existing violations in files this commit never touched.

problems.description: GET /tasks response envelope changed from a bare array to {"data", "next_cursor", "total"} — a breaking API change. Consistent across repo and tests, so acceptable here, but callers outside the codebase would break silently.
count() runs a second full COUNT query on every page request; keyset/cursor pagination typically omits total to keep cost O(page) rather than O(all rows).
Pagination tests reset the shared Redis-backed limiter counters mid-test (every 50 posts) to avoid coupling — pragmatic but fragile; matches the SonarQube +1 smell / +25 cognitive complexity delta.
Ordering silently changed from created_at DESC to id DESC for pagination stability; tasks sharing created_at now sort differently than before the commit.

strengths: Clean keyset pagination using the limit+1 fetch trick to detect has_more without a second query, documented in the repository docstring
Rate limiting keyed per authenticated user with IP fallback for anonymous register/login endpoints
Reuses existing repository helpers (_fetch_all/_fetch_one) and preserves the repository/route layering pattern
Tests updated consistently and a new pagination suite added; limiter.reset() in conftest prevents Redis counter leakage between tests
New config exposed as UPPER_CASE env-overridable constants and functions are snake_case with type hints
commit_reviews.summary: A well-structured cross-cutting commit (rate limiting + keyset pagination) that respects existing repository layering and ships updated tests, though the 0.65 mechanical convention score reflects pre-existing violations in celery_app.py/celery_config.py/__init__.py that this diff does not touch — the commit's own code is convention-clean, so the two disagree.

compounding_issues: Session 1's `init_db()` at import time became a migration hub: sessions 2-4 kept appending schema migrations (owner_id, email, legacy-user seeding) into it, so every import now runs PRAGMA introspection plus conditional ALTERs, and session 5's import-time Limiter had to rely on in-memory fallback to stay test-friendly

Session 5's pagination made `get_tasks()`/`TaskRepository.get_tasks` dead code with a conflicting ordering rule (`created_at DESC` vs the new `id DESC`), leaving a latent ordering drift the same list endpoint would see if the dead path were ever resurrected

The session 2 legacy-compat user (random-hash 'legacy' account that absorbs pre-existing tasks) had to be manually preserved through sessions 3 and 4's schema changes, adding migration surface every subsequent session had to carry

Pagination ordering by `id DESC` relies on autoincrement ids matching insertion order, which the session 2 `created_at DESC` ordering of the same data does not guarantee — two incompatible orderings of one list endpoint coexist
key_decisions: Session 2's JWT auth + per-user `owner_id` task ownership transformed the seed's single-tenant todo API into a multi-tenant one, using a legacy-compat user to migrate pre-existing seed rows instead of orphaning them

Session 4's repository extraction (BaseRepository generic CRUD + TaskRepository/UserRepository) cleanly decoupled SQLite from routes, shrinking app.py by ~126 lines and giving session 5's pagination a clean seam to build on

Session 3's Celery-based completion notification fired only on a genuine pending->completed transition (bug caught by a test that revealed repeated completed PUTs would spam emails), with `.delay` monkeypatchable so the suite needs no live broker
Session 5's rate limiter keyed on the JWT subject with an IP fallback and an in-memory fallback storage, keeping the whole test suite Redis-free while rate-limiting real deployments
Test-first discipline from session 1: every session grew tests using tmp_path/monkeypatch isolation, and the 9-test suite stayed green through all four feature/refactor sessions
story_review.trajectory_description: Quality improved monotonically across all five sessions, forming an unusually clean arc. Session 1 was a conservative hardening pass (timezone-safe timestamps, validation, WSGI-safe init) that also planted the first test suite. Session 2 was the riskiest and largest leap, introducing JWT auth, multi-tenant ownership, and an idempotent schema migration for the seed data. Session 3 integrated Celery async notifications and used its own tests to surface and fix a real edge-case bug (duplicate notification on repeat completions), showing the tests earning their keep. Session 4 was a behavior-preserving refactor that extracted a generic repository layer, and Session 5 crowned the arc with cross-cutting concerns — cursor pagination and auth-aware rate limiting — backed by new validation tests and updated response contracts. The codebase ends production-shaped rather than accreted, with a thin Flask layer over repositories, no live-infrastructure test dependencies, and a fully green suite.
story_review.summary: A textbook 5-session story: a hardening pass, a bold-but-migrated auth/ownership feature, an async integration that caught a real bug via tests, a clean repository refactor, and cross-cutting pagination/rate-limiting — a near-flawless linear progression ending in a production-shaped, fully-tested API.
